newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Germany keen to upgrade Bosnia peacekeeping role.
newsitem.headline: Germany keen to upgrade Bosnia peacekeeping role.

text.p: Germany is keen to participate fully in further peacekeeping duties in Bosnia and wants to deploy troops in the former Yugoslav republic, Defence Minister Volker Ruehe said in Sarajevo on Wednesday.
Ruehe said a new international peacekeeping mandate in Bosnia to succeed that of the NATO-led peace Implementation Force (IFOR), which expires on December 20, should be limited to a year.
"It is clear there will be a new mandate and Germany will show solidarity and play a meaningful part," Ruehe told reporters.
He has made clear he wants German troops to play a full role in international peacekeeping missions after decades of avoiding military involvement abroad.
Deployment of German troops to former Yugoslavia is an especially sensitive issue because of Germany's World War Two occupation of the Balkans.

Ruehe, speaking during a joint visit to German and British troops in Bosnia and Croatia with British Defence Secretary Michael Portillo, said he was not pressing for a German to be in command of peacekeeping forces.
But Ruehe he wants his country's armed forces to take a more mainstream role in Bosnia if the international peacekeeping mandate is extended, which is widely expected.

Portillo said a meeting of NATO defence ministers in Norway next week could take the first step towards a decision on whether to form a follow-on peace force in Bosnia. Consultations would be held with non-NATO nations in IFOR too.
"If there is a NATO decision to have a follow-on force, the United States would have to be a part of it. NATO came in together, NATO is serving together and NATO will leave together," he said.
Britain has contributed a contingent of more than 9,000 troops and the United States about 15,000 to the 53,000-strong IFOR. About 4,000 German support troops are based in Croatia.
Germany has said it would be prepared to contribute infantry peacekeepers with armoured vehicles to a force that could succeed IFOR.
Portillo said he and Ruehe also wanted to assess the outcome of Bosnia's first postwar general elections.

Bosnian President Alija Izetbegovic, a Moslem, won the race for the senior seat on the country's new three-man collective presidency, followed by Serb nationalist Momcilo Krajisnik and Croat nationalist Kresimir Zubak.

"The elections represent in themselves an enormous step forward on the road to peace," Portillo said. "There was concern as to how the elections would be conducted, whether they would bring violence and killing."
Ruehe called for Bosnia's factions to set up joint institutions without delay.
"Friendship and peace cannot be commanded, it must come from within, from the responsible politicians. That's the next important step," he said.
